title: Spy Shots Reveal New Dirt-Focused BMW M 1300 GS On The Way - ADV Pulse
content: BMW’s “M” badge has long signaled top‑tier performance in the automotive world, and in recent years it has made a decisive move into BMW Motorrad’s lineup with the M 1000 RR, M 1000 R, and M 1000 XR. BMW trademark filings back in 2022 suggested that a higher-spec ‘M’ version of the R 1300 GS may be on the way. Now, it appears the brand is finally ready to expand the M family with the introduction of a new flagship adventure motorcycle. Although BMW has never officially confirmed an M 1300 GS, new sightings around the company’s development facilities strongly suggest the model is entering the final stretch of testing. A covered prototype — transported under a tarp for secrecy — has been photographed by moto-paparazzo Bernhard M. Höhne, indicating the bike is already in an advanced stage of development. Early prototypes typically lack cosmetic details like labeling, but the overall form points to a machine nearing production readiness. Unlike the previous R 1250 GS HP variant, which was largely a cosmetic package, the upcoming M 1300 GS appears to be a significant redesign aimed at off‑road performance. The most notable change is a shift to 21‑inch front and 18‑inch rear spoke wheels, similar to the air/oil‑cooled R 12 G/S, signaling BMW’s intent to position the M model as an even more dirt‑capable GS. The prototype was fitted with Metzeler Karoo tires, and additional visible updates include what appears to be longer suspension travel, a reinforced and revised final‑drive swingarm support, and high‑performance M‑brakes with the signature blue finish. Unlike the R 1300 GS Adventure, the M model is likely to use the smaller R 1300 GS fuel tank to save weight and improve mass distribution. The 1300cc water‑cooled boxer engine appears largely unchanged from the R 1300 GS. Its already stout 110 ft-lbs of torque @ 6,500 RPM should remain more than adequate. Engineers might squeeze out a few more horsepower beyond the R 1300 GS’s 145 hp @ 7,750 RPM, but this wouldn’t really be necessary, especially since the M 1300 GS is expected to shed weight through body changes and premium materials such as titanium, likely used in the exhaust system. Styling changes remain speculative, but a revised seat is being rumored, and a reworked rear frame is expected. The removal of front and rear radar units also wouldn’t be surprising, as it would reduce weight and align with the M model’s more off road-driven mission. Overall, BMW appears to be aiming the M 1300 GS as the most aggressive off-road variant of the GS lineup — less travel‑enduro, more high‑performance machine capable of tackling any terrain. As with BMW’s other M‑series motorcycles, the M 1300 GS is expected to sit at the top of the boxer range in both capability and price. For context, the M 1000 XR and M 1000 R run about $8,000-$12,000 more than their next‑closest variants, suggesting the M 1300 GS may follow a similar pricing gap. Before the M model arrives, BMW is reportedly preparing a mild update to the R 1300 GS, possibly as early as early fall. The updated GS with standard cast wheels was also spotted alongside the M prototype and serves as a useful comparison point for the changes underway. title: Selena Gomez, Benny Blanco, and Becky G’s 'Te Olvido (La La)' Lyrics Are About Ending a Situationship - ELLE
content: Over a year after releasing I Said I Love You First, Selena Gomez and Benny Blanco have teamed up again—this time with Becky G—for Blanco’s upcoming Spanish album Hermoso. The trio released “Te Olvido (La La)” (in English: “I’m Forgetting You (La La)”) last night. In the Spanish lyrics, a woman asks her partner to define their relationship once and for all—or risk being left for good. Becky G and Gomez ask the man in the chorus, “Amor mío, ¿qué tienes conmigo? / Que no me quieres con nadie, pero tampoco contigo / Dime si somo’ o no somo’ de una vez, te lo pido / Y así yo decido si te quiero o te olvido.” (“My love, what is your deal with me? / You don’t want me with anyone else, but you don’t want me with you either / Tell me once and for all if we’re a thing or not, I’m asking you / That way I can decide whether to love you or forget you.”) In the verses, they call out his lies and questionable behavior, with Gomez telling him in the second verse not to trifle with her: “Tú estás pa’ darle a fuеgo / No digo na’, aunque to’ lo veo / Porque en la mierda yo también juego, bebé.” (“You’re all about playing with fire / I don’t say a word, even though I see it all / ’Cause I play dirty too, baby.”) The song, written by Blanco, Becky G, and Gomez, doesn’t seem to be directly about their love lives, though it might have been inspired by their pasts. Blanco and Gomez are married. Becky G, meanwhile, spoke on an April episode of Call Her Daddy about calling off her engagement to soccer player Sebastian Lletget amid cheating rumors in 2023. She said they are back together now, though it took work to rebuild their relationship. She’d still “love to” marry him someday. “Like, re-propose to me,” she said, via People. The hardship changed her, she added: “Post-traumatic growth is a choice. I do think that there is a shift in mentality that happened for me where it was like, I don’t want to be a victim of anything.” “Te Olvido (La La)” captures a woman refusing to be a victim and getting her own situationship out of purgatory. title: The Internet Says Karol G’s New Album Cover Looks Like Britney Spears’ In the Zone but Is That Really a Problem? - BELatina
content:
Karol G announced her upcoming album “No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto,” set for release on August 7th, 2026, and the internet immediately had opinions that had nothing to do with the music. The promotional cover art, dominated by blue tones, soft lighting and a pose that reminded many viewers of Britney Spears’ “In the Zone” era from 2003, sent social media into a debate about whether the Colombian artist was plagiarizing or paying homage to one of pop music’s most iconic visual aesthetics. The answer, for anyone who has been paying attention to Karol G’s career, is neither complicated nor controversial. Karol G has said in multiple interviews that Britney Spears was one of her biggest inspirations growing up, which makes the visual similarities on this album cover feel less like coincidence and more like a deliberate artistic choice. Whether she has explicitly confirmed that this specific cover references the “In the Zone” era or not, the context of her career and her publicly stated admiration for Spears makes the conversation about plagiarism feel particularly ungenerous. Calling it theft misunderstands how art actually works. Inspiration, reference and homage are not theft. They are how culture moves forward, how artists locate themselves within a lineage of people who shaped them, how they say thank you to the ones who came before. The people demanding outrage over a blue-tinted album cover that evokes early 2000s pop aesthetics need to take a breath. Art has always built on what came before it. Painters reference painters. Filmmakers quote filmmakers. Musicians absorb the sounds and images of the artists who formed them and eventually make something new from that inheritance. Karol G grew up watching Britney Spears redefine what a pop star could look like, sound like and feel like, and she has never pretended otherwise. An album cover that channels that energy is an artist honoring her roots, and the people celebrating the reference on social media understand something the critics do not: influence is not imitation. Karol G has built one of the most successful careers in the history of Latin music by absorbing her influences and transforming them into something distinctly her own, and this album appears to be a conscious nod to the era that shaped her before she reshaped an entire genre. The comments circulating online range from enthusiastic recognition to manufactured outrage, with fans writing things like “It’s giving Britney Spears In the Zone” while others celebrate the return of an aesthetic rooted in early 2000s pop. The ones celebrating it are closer to the truth. While the album cover debate consumed social media, Karol G’s Viajando Por El Mundo TropiTour was generating its own headlines for reasons considerably more compelling. During one of her tour dates, she invited a five-year-old girl named Khloé onto the stage. Khloé was attending her first concert, and when Karol G asked her what her favorite song was, the child answered with complete honesty: “Dai Dai,” the Shakira song from the 2026 World Cup. Rather than being fazed by the response, Karol G smiled, stopped the show and performed a fragment of the song alongside the little girl, encouraging the entire audience to join them. The reaction across social media was overwhelmingly positive, with fans praising the naturalness with which she turned a potentially awkward moment into one of the most memorable of the tour. The moment said everything about who Karol G is as a performer: someone secure enough in her own identity to celebrate another artist’s song in the middle of her own concert because a five-year-old asked her to. The people who want to turn the Britney comparison into a controversy are arguing against the basic premise of how artistic influence has worked across every creative discipline in human history. An album cover that evokes an era Karol G has openly admired deserves curiosity and appreciation rather than accusations of theft. Art has never existed in a vacuum and the artists who shaped us deserve to be honored in the work of those who came after them. August 7th cannot come soon enough. NO PURCHASE NECESSARY. content: Stay ahead of the curve and never miss out on what's fresh, exciting, and essential. Scan the QR code above to download the HYPE app now, or check it out in the app stores. Scan the QR code to open the article on your device or within the Hypebeast App. Karol G and Reebok are celebrating the power of Classics with “Born Classic. Worn Together.”, the latest chapter in her sneaker-forward Tropicoqueta era. As she takes the “Viajando Por El Mundo TropiTour” across the globe, the Colombian artist is stepping on stage in classic Reebok silhouettes. “La Bichota” announced her footwear ambassadorship in January 2026 and awaits her first collaborative line set to launch next year. Now, Karol G and Reebok officially unveil the “Born Classic. Worn Together.” campaign, celebrating the power of music, style, and movement to bring communities together. Shot in Mexico City, the campaign captures the vibrant spirit of her Tropicoqueta era through warm sunset tones and timeless Reebok Classics. “Tropicoqueta is about celebration, connection, and embracing your most authentic self, so it felt very special to bring that energy into this campaign. The visuals, the colors, the movement, and the people all reflect that same feeling of joy and freedom.” We caught up with Karol G to talk about “Born Classic. Worn Together.”, her partnership with Reebok, and how she’s taking her favorite kicks on tour. Why did you choose to join the Reebok family, and how does the brand align with your personal style? “Joining the Reebok family felt very natural because the brand has always represented authenticity, individuality, and self-expression. I’ve always believed that style is about showing who you are and feeling confident in what you wear, and that’s something I connect with deeply. Reebok allows people to express themselves in their own way, and I love being part of that.” How are you merging Colombia and Reebok through the “Born Classic, Worn Together” campaign? “For me, Colombia is a huge part of who I am, and I carry my culture with me everywhere I go. This campaign felt special because it celebrates the things that bring people together: music, style, movement, and shared experiences. I love being able to represent where I come from while connecting with people from different cultures and backgrounds around the world.” How does your latest Reebok campaign celebrate your recent Tropicoqueta album? “Tropicoqueta is about celebration, connection, and embracing your most authentic self, so it felt very special to bring that energy into this campaign. The visuals, the colors, the movement, and the people all reflect that same feeling of joy and freedom. It’s about celebrating individuality while also recognizing the things that bring us together.” “I dreamed about owning a pair of Reeboks growing up. They were so special then, and I remember being so happy when I received my first pair as a child. The Reebok Freestyle His are my favorite.” How do you want to introduce Reebok to Latin American audiences who connect with your music? “I want people in Latin America to see Reebok as a brand that feels connected to them and their own style. Our region is full of so much creativity, culture, and individuality, and I love how people use fashion to tell their stories. I hope people feel inspired to express themselves in their own way and make these pieces part of their everyday lives.” How will you be bringing Reebok with you on the “Viajando Por El Mundo TropiTour”? “Reebok sneakers are worn throughout my tour performances, both on me and many of my dancers. It is so magical seeing it all come to life. Official confirmation of the model had been lacking until recently, but that is no longer necessary: initial sightings in the vicinity of the Munich-based company’s development department suggest that development of the M1300 GS is entering the home straight: Although our photographer was unable to capture any photos of prototypes in action, the test bike – which was being transported under a tarpaulin to maintain secrecy – confirms that the model is at a very advanced stage. BMW is therefore unlikely to delay the launch for much longer. And even before that – possibly as early as early autumn – a subtle facelift is due for the best-selling R1300 GS, which can also be seen in our photos and serves as a point of comparison. The M1300 GS itself is set to become the flagship of the GS range and, unlike the 1000 models, is clearly positioned as being suitable for off-road use. Its roots go back to the original GS R80 G/S and its successes in the Paris-Dakar Rally. In an earlier conversation with our editor-in-chief Ivo Schützbach, BMW Motorrad CEO Markus Flasch hinted at its significance for an off-road-capable Boxer flagship: “Today, anyone who remembers motorbikes from back then has the Marlboro bike in mind, and the successes we achieved even back then with the M colours on the bike!” Whilst the design isn’t yet recognisable, key chassis components certainly are: unlike the HP version of its predecessor, the R1250 GS – which was essentially a visually adapted trim variant – the upcoming top-of-the-range GS model will undergo a thorough overhaul. Most strikingly, much like the air-cooled forerunner R80 G/S, it will feature off-road-style wheel sizes. This means a 21-inch front wheel and an 18-inch rear wheel – the prototype shown is fitted with Metzeler Karoo tyres. Hidden beneath the cover are also longer suspension travel and a sturdier, redesigned support for the swingarm. The more powerful M brakes, with their distinctive blue colour, are already clearly visible. It remains to be seen when the M1300 GS will arrive at dealerships – a launch before the 2027 season is likely. title: VAIV Company's AI-Powered Knowledge Management System Earns GS Grade 1 Certification - thelec.net
content: AI data company VAIV Company announced that its AI-based knowledge management system, VAIV KMS, has received Grade 1 Good Software (GS) Certification from the Korea Testing Laboratory (KTL), enabling the company to meet key requirements for participation in South Korea's public procurement market. GS Certification is a government-recognized software quality certification program established under Article 20 of the Software Promotion Act. Software products awarded GS Grade 1 certification are eligible for registration on the Public Procurement Service's KONEPS online procurement marketplace and can qualify for preferential purchasing by public institutions. VAIV Company describes VAIV KMS as an AI-powered knowledge management system that consolidates operational knowledge scattered across customer service centers and business departments, allowing employees to access relevant information when needed. According to the company, the system enables customer service representatives to retrieve information instantly without manually searching through large volumes of documents, including product guides, terms and conditions, and operational manuals. This can help reduce response times and improve consistency in customer service delivery. VAIV Company plans to use the GS Grade 1 certification as a springboard for expanding beyond the financial sector into public-sector knowledge management systems and citizen complaint-handling services. The company said its capabilities have already been validated in the financial industry, where K Bank is among its knowledge management system customers.

title: MISOINFO Tech's VLM-Based AI OCR Solution 'ViiX' Receives GS Grade 1 Certification - thelec.net
content: Multimodal data platform and AI company MISOINFO Tech announced on July 30 that its AI optical character recognition (OCR) solution, ViiX, has obtained Grade 1 Good Software (GS) Certification, South Korea's highest government-recognized software quality rating. ViiX is an AI OCR solution built on a Vision Language Model (VLM) architecture that enables simultaneous understanding of text and visual information. According to MISOINFO Tech, unlike conventional OCR systems that primarily focus on extracting text, ViiX analyzes documents and images comprehensively. The system can interpret document layouts, tables, images, contextual information and key-value data, allowing it to automatically structure a wide range of unstructured content, including medical records, manufacturing work instructions, semiconductor and construction process documents, contracts and public administration records. The company said the structured data generated by ViiX can subsequently be used for search, analytics, integration with generative AI applications and workflow automation. GS Grade 1 certification provides eligibility for preferential purchasing by public institutions and qualification for certain government procurement contracts. MISOINFO Tech said the certification formally validates the technology, quality and reliability of the ViiX platform, and the company plans to expand its business into public-sector, healthcare and manufacturing markets. It is also preparing an AI OCR appliance that can be deployed in various customer environments. The ViiX AI appliance combines AI OCR software with hardware optimized for both Nvidia GPU servers and domestically developed neural processing units (NPUs). The integrated system is designed for rapid deployment, requiring only power and network connectivity without complex installation procedures. MISOINFO Tech intends to supply the appliance to organizations operating on-premises environments in security-sensitive sectors, including government, defense, semiconductor manufacturing, finance and healthcare. The company is also pursuing an AI full-stack strategy by integrating ViiX with its SmartBIG Management Workflow platform and ACTIC AI orchestration platform, enabling customers to manage document recognition, AI analysis and workflow automation through a unified platform.

title: Former Bobby G’s employees and contractors point to pattern of missed payments and poor communication - The Oaklandside
content: East Bay matcha guide | A guide to the East Bay’s CSAs | Cenaduria Elvira is on the move UC Berkeley alum Calvin Miller was first drawn to Bobby G’s Pizzeria for its New York-style pizza and wide selection of draught beers. Before long, Bobby G’s became his neighborhood haunt for Sunday night NFL games, wings, and the occasional Wednesday trivia night, which was popular among college students. In May 2025, the opportunity arose to work at Bobby G’s as a server; Miller said that it felt like an easy decision. He signed some brief paperwork and joined the front-of-house staff the next day. It was shortly after getting his first paycheck that the problems started. “From that moment on, everything went downhill,” Miller said in an interview with Nosh, describing a pattern of delayed paychecks and poor communication about the late payments from restaurant owners Gurpreet Kaur and Gurmukh “Jay” Bansel Singh. Miller is not the only former employee of Bobby G’s to allege similar experiences. In March, the restaurant’s former social media coordinator, Jennifer Baquing, filed a lawsuit in the Alameda County Superior Court alleging wage violations, failure to reimburse business expenses and employee misclassification, among other complaints. Shortly afterwards, in April 2026, Bobby G’s closed indefinitely. Baquing named Game & Co, Inc – the corporate parent of Bobby G’s Pizzeria – and its shareholders, Singh and Kaur, as defendants. According to the complaint, Kaur and Singh “systematically” underpaid and withheld wages during her time of employment before terminating her year-long employment contract in late December 2025, well ahead of its Oct. 16, 2026 expiration date — a breach of her signed contract that insured compensation for early termination without proper notice or cause. Baquing and her attorney, Alexei Kuchinsky, declined to comment at this time. Over about 10 weeks from the end of May through July, East Bay Nosh tried to reach Kaur for comment via cellphone, the restaurant’s landline, email and a LinkedIn message, but he did not respond. On July 23, Bansel Singh sent Nosh a text message and email asking for Nosh to contact him. However, despite numerous follow-up attempts by us on that day, and leading up to publication of this report, including phone calls, text and email messages, Singh has not been in touch again. East Bay Nosh spoke with former employees, contractors and vendors who worked at or with Bobby G’s while it was run by Kaur and Singh. Similar to Baquing and Miller, they described a pattern of missed or delayed payments and erratic communication from ownership. The restaurant at 2072 University Ave. remains dark, and a “Now Leasing” sign has been posted in the window by Raj Properties. Bobby G’s first opened in late December 2006 as a small pizzeria owned by Berkeley native Robert Gaustad. Prior to Bobby G’s, Gaustad had lived in over 33 cities –working across film, food, and tech – before he returned home to pursue his dream of opening a restaurant. Gaustad and his partner, Heather Kratt, purchased the Indian-pizza fusion restaurant for sale on 2072 University Ave. in October 2006 and quickly got to work to bring their vision to life. “For me, if I was going to be in a restaurant that I own and work seven days a week in, for up to 12 hours a day, I wanted it to have the things that I like: sports, beer, and music,” said Gaustad who is also a blues harmonica player. With time, the result was a bustling sports bar that sold 13 beers on tap and pizza made from Bay Area-sourced ingredients like Giusto’s flour. “If your ingredients are poor, you can’t fix that, but we had good ingredients, good pizza and good chefs like Keith [McNabb],” Gaustad said. The space also offered an abundance of tabletop seating as well as cozy sofas pushed against the walls adorned with sports jerseys and framed photos of musicians. “It was Berkeley’s living room,” Berkeley photojournalist Aaron Rosenblatt told East Bay Nosh while scrolling through the photos he took of Bobby G’s throughout the last decade. “Anyone could sit as long as they didn’t cause trouble.” As shown by Rosenblatt’s photos, the restaurant went on to see Bogart, the neighborhood husky, regularly beg at the bar for chicken scraps, a crowd of locals raise a glass to chef McNabb — called “the greatest guy and punkrocker” by Gaustad after he passed away from cancer in 2017 — and the construction of an outdoors seating parklet, at no cost, by the Bobby G’s regular Tibor Lageman in 2020. Across those years, Bobby G’s weekly bluegrass jams and trivia nights continued to attract large crowds, as did the annual release of the limited-edition Pliny the Younger beer from the Russian Brewing Company. On the Pliny release day at Bobby G’s, a heavily congested line would form down University Avenue and around Citibank, with people hailing from across the East Bay. During one year’s release, recalled by Gaustad, the keg ran dry in only 47 minutes. “I did the 10-ounce pours, lined them up, over and over, and suddenly it was over,” much to the chagrin of those who remained in line for the coveted beer. In 2016, Gaustad sold Bobby G’s to the brothers Karan and Randeep Rekhi after a dispute with the restaurant’s landlord, Raj Properties, which did not respond to multiple requests for comment. While the neighborhood haunt survived multiple ownership changes and the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic, trouble emerged after the 2024 handoff to Kaur and Singh, according to multiple Bobby G’s contractors and employees. In February 2025, the owner of Trivia CA, Chris O’Brien — who is also the partner of Jennifer Baquing, who filed the lawsuit — received a direct message on Instagram from the former Bobby G’s trivia hosts who warned him of delayed payments from Kaur and Singh. O’Brien, who was considering a job offer from Bobby G’s at the time, said he raised the issue of delayed payments during his first meeting with management on March 19, 2025. Management allegedly assured him: “There’s not going to be any problem paying you.” For the first few months, O’Brien said that his payments arrived mostly on time. Trivia nights boomed under O’Brien’s watch with the average number of players increasing from 40 to 80, and sometimes 120 on the most crowded nights. Despite the buzz, O’Brien said his payments began to habitually fall behind schedule, and he regularly had to remind ownership to send him his fees. East Bay Nosh reviewed screenshots of text messages between Singh and O’Brien, supplied to us by O’Brien, that corroborated the pattern of delayed payments and subsequent excuses from ownership. O’Brien departed in January 2026 due to the financial strain and stress. While he received the money owed to him in the end, others did not have the same experience. Berkeley resident Ian Powell, a professional brewer, alleges that Kaur and Singh contracted him to design and rebuild a cold box with a direct draw system (a refrigerated cabinet for dispensing beer on tap) for the restaurant in July 2024. According to Powell, all parties agreed that he would receive $8,000 as outlined by the estimate. Powell described the relationship as initially positive, recalling comments from Singh like, “Man, my dude, I can’t wait to work with you.” But the arrangement later deteriorated. Powell said that on multiple occasions Kaur and Singh failed to show up to let him into the restaurant to continue his work, leaving him and his business partners stranded while calls went unanswered. Powell said the final blow came when Kaur paid only $1,000 despite the completed designs and contractor coordination. Powell was then unable to complete the job. “They frosted me out of the place and made it clear they didn’t have the money to pay,” Powell said. Miller, the former server, said that, in addition to consistently late payments and bounced checks, the work environment was unhealthy in other ways. For example, employees were not given regular breaks as mandated by California Labor Law, and the owners would dodge their calls and communications regarding the payments. Two former Bobby G’s employees who did not wish to speak on the record corroborated Miller’s account of late payments and poor communication from management. “It got to a point where I said, I won’t come to work until I’m paid,” Miller said. He eventually gave his final warning to ownership that he would quit if he didn’t receive his next payment on time. Miller said his next payment was delayed by a week, forcing him to borrow money from a roommate for his graduation cap and gown. He quit in November 2025. Baquing was hired to be the social media manager for Bobby G’s in April 2025. The lawsuit claims that although Baquing was working as an employee, ownership misclassified her as a contractor in order to “evade their obligations under California wage-and-hour laws.” The lawsuit also claims Baquing was routinely paid “days or weeks late,” and multiple checks issued to her were returned for insufficient funds, while also alleging Kaur and Singh improperly commingled Game & Co Inc’s funds with their own funds and diverted assets from the business to themselves. Baquing signed a new one-year contract also signed by Kaur that was to run from Oct. 16, 2025 to Oct. 16, 2026 and included, among several provisions, stipulations on payment, pay frequency, and an early termination fee. Then, the lawsuit claims, on Dec. 18, 2025, Kaur and Singh “unilaterally terminated [Baquing] without cause, without notice, and without paying the contractually obligated early termination compensation,” amounting to $90,600. While the lawsuit filed by Baquing makes its way through court, Bobby G’s now sits empty, waiting for a new tenant. An initial case management hearing is scheduled for Oct. 6, 2026. The news of its closure saddened Gaustad, who called the restaurant his “baby.” “We worked hard to build that place and clientele, and we made a lot of lifelong friends doing it,” he said. Gaustad is now retired in Petaluma but had looked forward to visiting Bobby G’s this December for what would have been the pizzeria’s 20th anniversary. Gaustad said that he and Singh had even texted briefly about throwing a celebration to commemorate two decades of Bobby G’s history. “I wish it had lasted longer and I think it would have, if people had kept the quality and kept doing the right thing,” said Gaustad. It wouldn't be The Boy's first time dabbling in the Latin world. The Canadian rapper has joined forces with the likes of Bad Bunny, Romeo Santos, and, most recently, Chino Pacas. He first flexed his Spanish skills by crooning his verse alongside Romeo on their 2014 track "Odio," produced by Rico Love. Later, in 2018, Drake joined forces with El Conejo Malo on "MIA," where he rapped his verse in Spanish. The two reunited in 2023 for "Gently" off Drake's album For All The Dogs. He also has two songs with Chino Pacas, "Modo Capone" with Fuerza Regida and "Meet Your Padre" with PARTYNEXTDOOR. from their joint album $ome $exy $ongs 4 U. Karol G also has some crossover experience under her belt. Her most notable hip-hop collaboration to date is "Tusa" featuring Nicki Minaj. title: Karol G's concert fan moment takes an unexpected turn over Shakira's 'Dai Dai' - HOLA
content: Karol G shared a heartwarming and hilarious exchange with a young fan during her recent concert in Toronto after inviting the child onstage and asking a simple question: "What's your favorite song?" The answer caught everyone, including the Colombian superstar, completely off guard. Instead of naming one of Karol G's biggest hits, the young fan enthusiastically replied that her favorite song was "Dai Dai" by Shakira, the official anthem for the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The memorable interaction happened during Karol G's Toronto stop on her "Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour." As part of her concert tradition, the singer invited a young girl on the side of the stage and chatted with her in front of thousands of fans. Karol G asked the child what her favorite song was, likely expecting to hear one of her own tracks. Instead, she confidently answered, "Dai Dai." The singer paused for a moment before realizing the little fan was referring to Shakira's World Cup anthem. According to videos shared across social media, the audience immediately reacted with laughter and cheers as Karol G smiled through the unexpected moment. Rather than appearing embarrassed or disappointed, Karol G embraced the situation. She encouraged the young fan to sing part of "Dai Dai," and thousands of concertgoers happily joined in, transforming what could have been an awkward exchange into a joyful celebration of music. Social media clips show Karol G smiling as the audience sang along with the child. The interaction quickly spread across Instagram, TikTok, and other platforms, with many fans praising Karol G for handling the moment gracefully. The viral clip generated positive reactions online, with many viewers applauding the singer's sense of humor and relaxed attitude. Some fans joked that the little girl had confused Colombia's two biggest global music stars, while others pointed out that children often answer questions with complete honesty. Rather than correcting or dismissing the fan, Karol G let the moment unfold naturally, which many viewers said made the interaction even more genuine. Although the young fan chose a Shakira song, the moment also reminded fans of the connection between the two Colombian artists. Karol G and Shakira previously collaborated on the hit "TQG," one of the biggest Latin music releases of 2023. While rumors about rivalry between the singers have occasionally surfaced online, Karol G's reaction during the concert suggested there was no reason for the situation to become uncomfortable. Instead, she allowed the audience to enjoy the unexpected moment. The fan interaction arrived during an exciting stretch for Karol G. During the same Toronto concert, she also surprised attendees by announcing her upcoming album, "No Me Arrepiento De Sentir Tanto," which is scheduled for release on August 7. © ¡HOLA! title: Why Mikaela Shiffrin Keeps Going: Curiosity, GS and Super-G - Ski Racing Media
content: Mikaela Shiffrin has collected enough victories, medals and crystal globes to fill several remarkable careers. Yet the most successful alpine ski racer in history says those numbers reveal little about why she continues. In her YouTube video, “Why Do You Keep Going? | My Honest Answer,” Shiffrin offers an unusually open account of her current thinking. The solo episode of her “What’s the Point?” series explores motivation, retirement, giant slalom, super-G and the demanding offseason hidden behind her public appearances. Her answer to the question surrounding the next stage of her career comes down to one word: curiosity. “I just want to learn what’s around the corner,” Shiffrin said. “And I want to see if the work that I do right now can impact what’s around the corner in a positive way.” At 31, Shiffrin understands why questions about retirement have become more valid. She also leaves little doubt about her immediate intentions. Shiffrin recited a career résumé that includes 110 World Cup victories, 168 World Cup podiums and 18 crystal globes. She also listed three Olympic gold medals and 15 world championship medals, including eight golds. Reading those achievements aloud made her uncomfortable. “It’s cool, but it’s hard to connect with it,” Shiffrin said. Her latest season added another extraordinary chapter. She won nine of 10 slaloms and secured the discipline title before the end of January. She also earned her sixth overall globe and returned to the top of the Olympic slalom podium. Still, statistics cannot recreate the sensation of solving a technical problem, finding speed in training or producing the turns she imagined during Olympic pressure. For Shiffrin, that connection remains more meaningful than any numerical milestone. “It’s always been about the turns,” she said. “That’s what I can feel.” Her Olympic slalom victory provided the clearest example. Shiffrin carried a substantial advantage into the second run but refused to ski protectively. “I skied my heart out,” Shiffrin said. “It was the best run of slalom that I’ve ever done on that stage.” She took the risk that her approach might not work. The reward came from skiing the turns she wanted in the sport’s biggest environment. The gold medal confirmed the result, but the skiing gave the moment its meaning. Shiffrin’s slalom dominance commanded the brightest spotlight, but her progress in giant slalom may have carried greater personal significance. While rebuilding after her November 2024 crash in Killington, Vermont, Shiffrin fell to 30th in the giant slalom World Cup Start List rankings. By the end of the 2025-26 season, she had climbed back into the top seven and ranked fourth. Shiffrin called that recovery “a monumental step” for herself and her team. Shiffrin believes the level of women’s giant slalom has risen since she won her last discipline globe. She described the current field as more powerful and faster, with athletes performing at an exceptionally high level. Rather than finding that development discouraging, she finds it exciting. “I don’t know if I can consistently win GSs or win at all,” she said. “There were moments this past season where I felt like that level was within reach.” At other times, she questioned whether she could reach it. Shiffrin returned to several super-G races during the season. She described those starts as exhilarating, nerve-racking and extremely challenging. Still, the same thought arrived whenever she crossed the finish line. That reaction told Shiffrin she still had something to pursue in the event. She also recognizes how much work remains. Shiffrin said she needs improvement in several clear areas before she can become competitive in super-G. Much of that progress, she believes, will come through repetition and greater exposure to speed. Her brain must relearn how to process the gates, terrain, snow and other demands that arrive at a faster pace. The outcome remains uncertain. Once again, that is part of the attraction. Shiffrin also explained why alpine skiing can remain difficult for casual audiences to understand. Athletes try to recreate the conditions they expect to encounter. However, weather and snow can transform a race. A snowstorm may arrive. Temperatures can rise or fall. Fog can move onto the course between start numbers. Cloud cover can turn a bright track dark within minutes. Shiffrin said those changes can create a difference of five-tenths to a full second. That margin may separate a victory from third, fifth or even 10th place. Many of the variables remain outside an athlete’s control. That unpredictability makes ski racing difficult to explain and forecast. It also ensures that athletes must keep adapting. Even after 16 World Cup seasons, Shiffrin can still encounter something new. Shiffrin’s search for growth extends beyond skiing. During a packed week in New York, she participated in two live recordings of “What’s the Point?” and attended the ESPYS, the TIME100 Sports Gala, Fanatics Fest, sponsor appearances and the FIFA Club World Cup final. Those appearances may look glamorous from the outside. Shiffrin experiences them differently. She described herself as a natural introvert who feels more comfortable behind a helmet and goggles than making small talk on a red carpet. She compared entering a crowded event to walking into a school cafeteria without knowing where to sit. However, those uncomfortable experiences have helped Shiffrin recognize how many people remain unfamiliar with alpine skiing. She views that limited awareness as an opportunity. Her podcast and other projects may help introduce the sport to a broader audience. Her platform also allows her to discuss subjects that matter to her, including grief, post-traumatic stress disorder, mental health, access to sports, cancer research and climate change. Shiffrin recently appeared on Anderson Cooper’s “All There Is” podcast. She said the responses from listeners gave meaning to a conversation that required her to revisit painful experiences. Her skiing created the platform. She does not want to take it for granted. Shiffrin also addressed a persistent misconception about the life of an elite ski racer. After the Olympics, she still had six weeks of racing. Once the season ended, equipment testing followed. June and July then brought an intensive strength and conditioning block. Shiffrin commonly trains twice a day for a combined four to six hours. Media appearances and sponsor commitments fit around those sessions, not in place of them. Her team even considers proximity to a properly equipped gym when selecting lodging. Next comes Southern Hemisphere training before Shiffrin returns to Europe in October for final preparation ahead of the World Cup season. Once racing begins, the circuit moves between countries and occasionally continents until late March. The schedule leaves Shiffrin only four or five weeks a year at her Colorado home. It also limits her concentrated time with fiancé Aleksander Aamodt Kilde, who follows his own training and racing schedule with Norway. Because the women’s and men’s tours usually compete at different venues, the couple receives little uninterrupted time together. Shiffrin said they have not started planning their wedding. The delay does not trouble her. “I know who I want to spend my life with,” she said. For now, they value the limited time they can spend together. Shiffrin has achieved more World Cup success than any alpine ski racer in history. She does not believe that means skiing has nothing left to offer. She wants to learn whether she can reach another level in giant slalom. She wants to discover what greater repetition could unlock in super-G. She also wants to use her platform to bring more attention to alpine skiing and to subjects that matter beyond racing. The records describe what Shiffrin has accomplished. “I simply love skiing,” she said. “And I still feel like there’s more in that.” This article is based on Mikaela Shiffrin’s YouTube video, “Why Do You Keep Going? | My Honest Answer,” published as part of her “What’s the Point?” series. title: BMW F900 GS Adventure: Long-legged tourer, off-road giant, or both? - ca.news.yahoo.com
content: The rise of adventure bike sales in the UK seems as unstoppable as the rugged, knobby-tyred bikes themselves: latest figures show this segment rising by just over 20 per cent in June 2026, compared to the same month last year. It must be the call of the wild - even when the road runs out, you can keep on riding. In June 2025 2,389 new adventure bikes were registered, rising to 2,871 this year, according to the MCIA (Motorcycle Industry Association). It was a good month all-round; 'modern classics' sales rose just over 23 per cent, 'road sports' by over 22 per cent. By contrast, 'touring' model sales were down nearly 40 per cent. I had plenty of time to ponder this - and wonder whether I was on the 'right' bike - when I spent hours in the saddle of BMW's F900 GS Adventure model, on a 700-mile tour from London to the pretty Gwynedd coast and back. In the heatwave. The ride included hours of boring M4 to reach the Severn Crossing, then beautifully sinuous, undulating roads but, on this trip, no off-road sections which, with its 21-inch front wheel, 230mm of fork and 215 mm rear suspension travel, 230mm of ground clearance, optional Enduro Pro riding mode and off-road swagger, the F900 looked cut out for. Strange, then, that in BMW Motorrad's UK sales blurb, there are no images of the F900 braving deserts, mountains, river crossings; the closest it gets is when it's parked artistically in a summer meadow. Instead, the marketing material stresses the bike's suitability for 'adventure', 'touring', its readiness for 'all short and long trips', even, with the Ride Pro package, its compatibility with 'extensive touring'. Given that BMW has plenty of 'proper' tourers and that it also pitches the bigger, far costlier, heavier R 1300 GS, along with the F900 GS (non-Adventure model) very much as off-road machines, pictured being ridden in rocky streams, desert sand and on forest trails, it's hard to see exactly what kind of riding the F900 is aimed at. Replacing the F850 GS Adventure, the newcomer weighs just two kgs more, has more power (up from 95hp to 105hp), marginally more torque and is claimed to have snappier power delivery. The new bike has beefier, adjustable forks and enduro-style footpegs, perhaps suggesting more aptitude for the rough stuff. More goodies (heated grips, cruise control) now come as standard on the base model. Visually the new bike looks quite different; despite its engine crash bars and sump guard, it appears slightly less off-roady, more tour-y, especially with its 'blocky' panels flanking the tank. So how's it go? The first thing you notice is how heavy it is to heave off the side-stand. Park it carelessly on a camber so that it leans (its stand presents a steep angle anyway) and it can be a struggle getting vertical. It feels tall too, the standard seat height of 875mm leaving me (I measure up at around 5' 10 inches) on tip-toes, not great for tight manoeuvring. (The BMW lower seat option takes it to 825mm, with a further suspension mod taking it down as far as 805mm.) Once rolling, that sensation of top-heavy weight quickly disappears, although it never feels like a lightweight at low speeds. It filters well enough in London traffic however, the lofty seating position giving excellent views over and through traffic, the steering very nice and fluid. The review model came with large, extremely practical, official BMW 'tin' panniers and top box (same key as the huge 23-litre petrol tank, offering tons of space for a week's touring essentials, even if the right-hand-side pannier is slightly tighter to accommodate the high-rise (another nod to off-roading) exhaust. On the M4, the relaxed, low-revving nature of the parallel twin engine was welcome. Some critics say it's an unexciting engine with linear power delivery instead of - presumably more exciting - power 'bands'. I liked it. It pulled beautifully and sonorously from low revs, delivering nice big dollops of torque, vibey character and very usable acceleration for overtaking, even in high gears. It was reasonably comfortable, too, for an hour and a half or so, anyway, before contact points below the hips - and aches in my knees - made stopping for a cuppa enticing. There's an easy-to-operate manual screen that can be adjusted on the fly. With the dash reading 36 degrees I kept the screen down for more cooling and the air felt reasonably 'clean', with little buffeting. On the highest setting my crash helmet was quieter, with less wind rush, slightly less pressure on the chest. The seating 'triangle' - as everyone now calls it - was relaxed; no wrist or arm strain, no backache either. In traffic (possibly because I was activating the clutch lever with just two fingers, making it impossible to pull it all the way in), neutral was sometimes tricky to locate. Only by taking a fistful of clutch, lever right into the bar, could I coax the green light into action; irritating while parking in the burning sun. In Wales, on swooping mountain passes the F900 was highly enjoyable; fun to swing through bends, then open up the throttle to bring the pleasing, relaxing water-cooled motor on-song. I found no issue, on tighter, faster bends, or long sweeping ones, with the 21-inch front wheel. It's a fast enough bike, and the engine is very flexible indeed. The supple ride quality was a thing of beauty. On narrow back-country roads, with grass and gravel creating a loose ridge along the centre of the lanes, the bike remained poised, in its element. It's worth noting that the standard bike comes with traction control and two ride modes; rain and road. Buyers can add the Riding Modes Pro package that includes additional settings (Dynamic, Enduro and Enduro Pro) and that lets you pre-select up to four modes and assign them to a button on the handlebars. Would I have taken it off-road? Not a chance; I like a green lane as much as the next rider but when (not if), it went down, there's no way I could have hoisted the 246kg bike up again, not on my own. This was underlined on-tour twice when, unable to find the 'right' angle in tight mountain pull-in parking spots, my riding companion had to help me push it up off the side stand. I now weigh only 70kgs after recently completing four years of intensive cancer treatment but I'm fairly fit and work out in the gym. I'm not that feeble. A couple of stronger, 'sitter-onners' had the same trouble. So, a highly enjoyable bike on the move but beware if you want to wheel it in and out of a garage or slopey tight spot, if you have short legs or are prone to toppling when parking. I also found it too damn hot. Sure, the effective screen and the see-through 'aerofoils' above and to the side of the tank would be great in rain and winter, and we don't often get 36 degrees (or do we now?). But when the mercury rose, they created a superheated bubble of air from the engine which - when I hit central London after hours boiling up on the M4 - did me in. I think I had mild heat stroke; that's the trouble with layers of biking gear, including airbag 'vest' and long touring boots. I find it a hard bike to categorise. If you just want a tourer, you don't need the height. If you want to go off-road, you won't want that top-heavy tippy feeling - unless you're very good indeed. My guess is that - coming in at just £12,420 for the base F900 GS Adventure (lots more if you want various goodies such as extra riding modes added on), it must be aimed at temping those who can't or won't spend £18,890 on the grander 1300 model. But that bigger bike has tricks up its sleeve including a lower centre of gravity (with that low-down 'boxer' engine) and 'adaptive vehicle height control' that automatically drops the height by 30mm shortly before a stop. If its bigger shaft-drive 1300 brother doesn't appeal however and you swivel back to the chain-drive F900 GSA, it faces very stiff competition from the likes of Triumph's 900 Rally Pro, Suzuki's V-Strom 1050 DE, Honda's Africa Twin, KTM's 890 and a clutch of new Chinese offerings, at substantially less money. Possibly the more practical choice would be the non-Adventure F900 GS, which I've not yet ridden, but which is substantially different from the Adventure model, and has been well received by critics. I wanted to like this bike and did in the bends and to some extent on the m-way. I liked the high build quality and general comfort. But there was always the knowledge that - at some point - I'd have to stop, and plan carefully ahead - or start sweating - just to park and move off again. It's probably one for hard-core, tall, long-legged BMW enthusiasts who don't mind people asking 'why didn't you go for the 1300...' Bader reportedly drove his scooter into a fire engine last weekend. title: Mercury 91-89 Valkyries (Jul 29, 2026) Game Recap - ESPN
content: PHOENIX -- — Kahleah Copper scored 27 points and the Phoenix Mercury overcame a 13-point deficit to beat the Golden State Valkyries 91-89 on Wednesday night in the return from the All-Star break for both teams. Alyssa Thomas had 25 points, nine rebounds and eight assists, and DeWanna Bonner added 17 points, 10 rebounds and three blocks for the Mercury (11-18). They have won three straight following a five-game losing streak. The Valkyries (19-9), who lost 90-82 at home to Washington last time out, have lost back-to-back games and fell a half-game behind second-place Las Vegas. Copper was called for her sixth foul with 1:45 to play, the Mercury challenged and, after replay review, the call was upheld. Nine seconds later Kayla Thornton hit a 3-pointer that tied it at 82, but Bonner answered with two free throws with 1:27 remaining to take the lead for good. Cecilia Zandalasini fouled out with 16 points on 6-of-17 shooting for Golden State. Veronica Burton added 15 points and Kaila Charles had 10 points and a season-high 10 rebounds, her second career double-double and her first since 2021. Valkyries: Host Toronto on Sunday night. title: How SG.GS is Redefining Global Connectivity with an Execution-Centric Approach - The Fast Mode
content: The connectivity business is changing. On the surface, cross-border enterprise network expansion appears to be surging like never before, as industries become more globalized and workforces, operations, and systems become increasingly distributed. However, the reality is more nuanced: enterprises aren’t looking for simple wholesale access anymore. They are looking for connectivity partners who can move quickly, solve operational challenges in real time, and consistently turn network strategy into tangible business outcomes. An execution-centric approach to building enterprise networks is becoming increasingly popular for modern businesses, who are putting stronger emphasis on being able to deliver reliable connectivity, respond to changes quickly, and scale capacity seamlessly. The largest aspect of this – reliability – concerns the network infrastructure itself. A resilient network often features carrier-grade backbone connectivity, backed by strong SLAs and designed with route diversity, redundant subsea paths, and automated failover. Equally critical is responsiveness – enterprises need partners that can provide immediate, round-the-clock support during network disruptions and changes to ensure operations continue without interruption. A third factor is scale – undoubtedly, one of the most important considerations for fast-growing enterprises. Scale is no longer as simple as maintaining a broad footprint, but having a truly “ubiquitous” network underpinned by flexible capacity and intelligent interconnection, leveraging key capabilities such as elastic bandwidth options, rapid provisioning, dense ecosystem interconnection, and infrastructure capable of supporting new cloud and AI workloads. A fourth and final factor is flexibility. Businesses are increasingly opting for providers who offer customizable architectures, rapid provisioning, and agile models designed to accommodate shifting traffic demands, hybrid cloud environments, and multi-market expansion strategies. For many enterprises, execution ultimately comes down to responsiveness, how quickly providers can provision services, adapt to changing requirements, troubleshoot issues, and support expansion into new markets without adding operational friction. For Asia-headquartered wholesale carrier SG.GS, execution sits at the heart of their commercial expansion strategy. The company provides a suite of connectivity services, spanning IP Transit, Ethernet Private Line, DC Wave, Dedicated Internet Access, Cloud Connect, and IX Peering. They boast a colossal network footprint spanning key Asian cities, including Hong Kong, Kuala Lumpur, Singapore, and Tokyo, as well as several European, U.S., LATAM, and Australian points of presence. However, this scale is just one part of their transformational growth story – a journey that took the company from a simple web hosting platform to a rapidly expanding APAC-headquartered global connectivity provider. According to founder and CTO Heng Chai Tan, the company’s evolution has been driven by a steady commitment to operational delivery, with a focus on three core business tenets – namely agility, customer support, and regional expertise. “Over the last twenty years, we’ve seen immense global growth in connectivity services, a trend that SG.GS has grown alongside in becoming one of the region’s most connected network carriers,” says Tan. Too many providers still compete primarily on footprint and capacity. But enterprise customers today need partners that can execute quickly, adapt to changing requirements and solve operational challenges across markets. This is where we have focused SG.GS – combining regional expertise with engineering-led delivery and long-term customer partnerships. We seek to provide more than just wholesale access to our customers, but a wider strategic partnership centred around their evolving  business and infrastructure requirements. Executing across APAC requires more than footprint alone. Enterprises expanding across the region often face fragmented infrastructure environments, varying regulatory requirements, inconsistent last-mile capabilities, and rapidly shifting capacity demands. SG.GS has positioned itself around helping customers navigate that complexity through regional expertise, engineering-led delivery, and operational responsiveness. That operational model is supported by a network footprint spanning 200+ PoPs across 30+ markets, alongside strategic peering and infrastructure relationships with partners including NTT Communications, Tata Communications, SGIX, HKIX, and BBIX. By helping enterprises navigate local interconnection challenges, infrastructure gaps, and regional deployment complexities SG.GS has established a strong position across both established and emerging growth markets. Execution is ultimately driven by technical competence – but for SG.GS, this is reinforced by an equally strong customer support model. The company works closely with enterprises to design tailored network solutions aligned with specific performance, latency, and scalability requirements, while ensuring customers engage directly with engineers and commercial specialists who understand their markets, regulatory environments, and infrastructure constraints. “Great customer experience is not defined by standardized service delivery and general best practices,” says Ben Cooper, the company’s newly-appointed SVP of Global Network Strategy.“It is defined by the ability to build true partnerships with customers, remain technically responsive to their evolving needs, and design flexible, reliable network solutions that adapt across markets and use cases. Ultimately, it is about delivering networks not just for the customer, but with the customer.” Enterprises are increasingly valuing partners that can consistently translate network strategy into tangible operational outcomes. That focus on operational execution and customer delivery has increasing translated in to commercial momentum and industry recognition, including SG.GS’ double-win at The Fast Mode Awards 2025, which saw the company clinching both the Enterprise Growth Leader and Emerging Telco Brand titles, alongside big names such as Lumen and Indonesia’s Linknet. As enterprise connectivity requirements continue to evolve, SG.GS is positioning itself around a simple premise: growth is not defined by footprint alone, but by the ability to consistently execute for customers across increasingly complex global environments. Through a combination of regional expertise, engineering-led delivery, and customer-focused operational agility, the company continues to build momentum across APAC and key international markets. title: Historic Parity on the Line in GS at Road America - Sportscar365
content: Could Aston Martin, Toyota, become seventh different GS manufacturer to win in seven years at Road America? Road America has emerged as a bit of a wild card round for IMSA Michelin Pilot Challenge competitors the last several years. A total of 42 cars are entered for the Road America 120, split 28 GS and 14 TCRs, for the seventh round of the season. Six different manufacturers have won overall and in GS since 2020: McLaren, BMW, Mercedes-AMG, Chevrolet, Porsche and Ford. Of those six, all but Chevrolet are still active. Aston Martin or Toyota could continue the parity streak if either manufacturer wins their first Road America race, and both are coming off highs at Canadian Tire Motorsport Park. Aston Martin won its second straight pole, with Heart of Racing Team’s Hannah Greenemeier following Hannah Grisham as the fastest GS qualifier two weeks earlier at Watkins Glen. Then Toyota won the race in Canada with RAFA Racing’s Kiko Porto and Varun Choksey parlaying their pace into a first victory. The CTMP round shifted the GS title battle to where only 40 points covers the top three. McCumbee McAleer Racing’s Nate Cicero and Robert Noaker now lead by 30 points over Ibiza Farm Motorsport’s Michael Cooper and Moisey Uretsky, with AutoTechnic Racing’s Stevan McAleer and Austin Krainz just ten points further back in third. Tough recent weekends have dropped Turner Motorsport’s Dillon Machavern and Luca Mars and Winward Racing’s Bryce Ward slightly down the order, but still with enough time to claw back the deficit as they’re both within 190 points. TCR saw a new Road America winner last year with Hyundai back on top at the track for the first time since 2020; Bryson Morris and Mark Wilkins delivered the Elantra N TCR’s first win at the venerable 4.048-mile circuit. Morris and Mason Filippi have been the model of consistency in TCR this year, with two wins including last time out at CTMP and five podiums achieved in six races. That sees them 200 points clear of teammates Denis Dupont and Preston Brown. Although that 200-point gap is strong, a tough result for the No. 33 car could bring any of the next five cars into title contention, as they’re only covered by 80 points. Among the handful of changes throughout the grid, Celso Neto is listed alongside Eddie Gou in the No. 55 Gou Racing with Stallion Audi RS 3 LMS TCR. Both Medusa Motorsports and RVA Graphics by Speed Syndicate Motorsports return after at least one-race absences, while LAP Motorsports has entered the No. 6 rather than No. 30 Ford Mustang GT4. This has come after Ford Racing and Multimatic built up a new chassis, which was delivered to the team’s shop in Brownsburg, Ind. on Saturday. Scott Thomson and Clayton Williams will pilot the entry this weekend. Pilot Challenge teams have one practice Thursday, a second Friday morning before qualifying Friday afternoon, and race Saturday at 12:50 p.m. CST. In 2017 the Waltham School District built a new grade school accommodating 240 students. The student body has increased 34% in the subsequent years, creating the need to look at putting a referendum on the ballot in November to look at funding a possible $10 million expansion. According to school board member, Rachel Balestri, since COVID, mandates for additional services like therapists, school psychologists and counselors, as well as the increased enrollment have caused the administration to use space previously designated for future expansion. The increased tax burden on a $200,000 property would be $300. Another informational meeting is scheduled for next Wednesday evening at 6 at the Waltham Grade School. title: Fans Experience Opening Weekend of KAROL G’s Tour - Hudson Valley Press
content:
CHICAGO – Global recording artist KAROL G officially launched her “Viajando Por El Mundo TropiTour” this weekend with two consecutive nights at Soldier Field in Chicago, welcoming more than 90,000 fans throughout the opening weekend. Marking the debut of her largest live production to date, “Viajando Por El Mundo TropiTour” invites audiences into a bold new live experience inspired by the vibrant spirit of Tropicoqueta. More than a concert, opening weekend marked the beginning of a journey that invites audiences around the world to celebrate the music, rhythms and spirit that continue to connect generations across Latin culture. From the opening moments, Soldier Field transformed into a world all its own. Across five acts, the production continuously evolved through immersive staging, live musicians, dynamic choreography and breathtaking visual moments, while pyrotechnics, fireworks and bursts of confetti amplified the energy throughout the night. Complementing the visual experience, KAROL G debuted a series of custom looks created in collaboration with Brett Alan Nelson, ETRO, Michael Schmidt Studios, The Blonds and SEKS, reflecting the bold, fashion-forward identity of the tour. Singer-songwriter Elena Rose opened both sold-out performances as the tour’s special guest, setting the stage for an unforgettable opening weekend. At the heart of the production, the now-signature pool served as one of the show’s defining visual elements, creating unforgettable moments as more than 90,000 fans sang, danced and celebrated together. One of the evening’s most memorable moments came as Academy Award-nominated actor Edward James Olmos appeared on screen to introduce the Tropicoqueta act, setting the stage for mariachi-inspired performances of “Ese Hombre Es Malo,” “200 Copas” and “MAMIII,” creating one of the production’s defining moments. Throughout the night, KAROL G moved effortlessly between reggaetón anthems, intimate ballads and reimagined versions of fan favorites. Fresh cumbia and salsa arrangements of “BICHOTA” and “TUSA” offered new interpretations of two of her biggest hits while keeping the audience on its feet from beginning to end. Opening night concluded with the debut of “MATADORA,” as KAROL G surprised fans with a special closing moment built around the new single, giving the Chicago audience its first introduction to the song before the show came to a close.
Following its sold-out opening weekend in Chicago, the tour continues across North America before traveling through Latin America and Europe, bringing KAROL G’s largest live production to audiences around the world.
